articles.title: This new qubit could be 100 times less error-prone in superfluid quantum computer breakthrough
articles.summary: A proposed qubit made with superfluid helium could cut quantum computing error rates by around 100 times by shielding quantum information from common forms of electromagnetic noise. If experiments confirm the predictions, the technology could eventually work alongside today’s superconducting qubits or serve as a new kind of quantum memory.

articles.title: Quantum computing’s “dark horse” just proved it can go universal
articles.summary: Researchers have shown that exotic quantum particles called non-Abelian anyons can perform the full range of operations needed for universal quantum computing. Using 54 qubits on Quantinuum’s H2 processor, they combined braiding and fusion to unlock capabilities that braiding alone could not provide.

articles.title: Scientists just made quantum computer operations 1,000 times faster
articles.summary: Researchers have found a way to perform certain quantum operations more than 1,000 times faster, cutting thousands of repeated control cycles down to just one. The advance could reduce errors and bring reliable, fault-tolerant quantum computers closer to reality.

articles.title: A “quantum bath” puts quantum entanglement on autopilot
articles.summary: Physicists have demonstrated a new way to entangle distant quantum bits without the constant measurements and active control normally required. The team created a “quantum bath,” a shared environment filled with correlated microwave photons that automatically pushes separated qubits into an entangled state and helps keep them there. The experiment confirms a theoretical prediction made more than 20 years ago and could offer a simpler way to connect modules in future quantum computers.

Nadella says we can no longer accept a world where AI is treated as a "set of nested black boxes" whose advice and actions we simply accept or […]

articles.title: DistroKid has been quietly taking down songs in response to UMG lawsuit
articles.summary: Artists are taking to social media to complain that DistroKid has unceremoniously removed their work without notice. Now DistroKid has confirmed to The Verge that the takedowns are a direct response to claims made by UMG. The label filed a lawsuit in September claiming that DistroKid has created an "AI-slop pipeline." Artists are saying that […]

His first successful presidential run was built on monikers like "Little Marco" and "Crooked Hillary"; he changed "fake news" from a phrase describing scammy media outlets to a derogatory term for the press at large. Over the past few weeks, he's clearly decided […]

articles.title: This light-powered AI can spot deepfakes with nearly 98% accuracy
articles.summary: UCLA researchers built an AI system that uses light to analyze more than a dozen videos simultaneously, detecting deepfakes with nearly 98% accuracy. Its speed, low energy demands, and resistance to attacks could make it a powerful tool for screening the growing flood of AI-generated video.

articles.title: MIT’s tiny flying robot gets 450% faster with AI
articles.summary: A new AI control system lets MIT’s tiny flying robot move with insect-like agility, boosting its speed by about 450 percent and allowing it to pull off 10 somersaults in 11 seconds. The technology could eventually enable miniature robots to search earthquake rubble and navigate dangerous spaces that conventional drones cannot reach.

articles.title: The shape behind the Einstein problem just revealed strange new physics
articles.summary: A mathematical shape famous for covering a surface without ever repeating has revealed an unexpected ability to twist light into unusual chiral patterns. The discovery could lead to new ways of controlling light, polarization, and advanced optical devices.

articles.title: AI uncovers hidden Ozempic side effects across 400,000 Reddit posts
articles.summary: AI analysis of 400,000 Reddit posts found that users of drugs such as Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro, and Zepbound reported unexpected symptoms including menstrual changes, chills, hot flashes, and fatigue. Researchers cannot say the medications caused these problems, but the patterns may reveal overlooked signals worth studying.

articles.title: Tiny nanolaser could cut computer energy use in half
articles.summary: Scientists have created an ultra-small nanolaser that could eventually allow microchips to transmit information with light instead of electricity, potentially making computers faster while cutting energy use roughly in half. Thousands of the lasers could fit on a single chip, opening possibilities for more efficient data centers, smartphones, and advanced medical sensors.

articles.title: High rare earth demand could complicate Europe's offshore wind ambitions
articles.summary: Wind turbines, devices that can convert energy from the wind into electricity, do not burn fuel during operation and could thus reduce greenhouse gas emissions. Despite their possible environmental advantages, building these devices depends heavily on the mines and factories supplying the metals they are made of.

articles.title: Can AI detect a silent internet outage before it occurs?
articles.summary: The internet can encounter a strange type of failure in which a router seems to function normally but silently drops some data packets. Network engineers refer to these issues as "black holes." In these cases, data enters the network, yet some of it vanishes without the router informing the network or the sender. Often, these problems go unnoticed until users start experiencing connection issues or data loss.

articles.title: 'Human-authored' book labels gain ground amid AI scandals
articles.summary: Initiatives to label books as written by humans, not artificial intelligence, are gaining ground following a string of scandals in which authors were suspected of using the technology without admitting it.

articles.title: A new approach to sustainable AI: Offloading part of the computational burden onto light
articles.summary: As artificial intelligence technologies become increasingly widespread, the growing demand for processing power and energy is emerging as a global challenge. Assistant professor Uğur Teğin from Koç University's Department of Electrical and Electronics Engineering has developed two new systems that use light itself, rather than conventional electronic circuitry, to perform computations for artificial intelligence. Published in two articles, the studies introduce new approaches to computing that could contribute to the development of faster and more energy-efficient AI systems.

articles.title: Global consensus sets testing guidelines for solar cells harvesting indoor light
articles.summary: Indoor photovoltaics (iPV) converts light from LEDs and fluorescent lamps found in homes and buildings into electricity, offering a route to self-powered sensors, remote controls, wearables and the tens of billions of connected devices expected to make up the internet of things (IoT). Whereas solar cells have had clear standards for measuring and reporting performance and stability outdoors under the sun, their use under indoor lighting has lacked a comparable consensus baseline standard.

articles.title: AI image watermarks can survive new model training, but durability varies by design
articles.summary: Watermarks are increasingly being used to make AI-generated images recognizable and to ensure their origin can be traced. Previous research has focused on whether watermarks can withstand image manipulation. CISPA researcher Michel Meintz from the SprintML Lab has investigated whether watermarks can withstand the training of a new generative model.

articles.title: Can salty, dirty water cool data centers? Research points to desalination as a cooling option
articles.summary: Data centers need water. And water byproducts from oil and gas and other industries need to go somewhere.

articles.title: Temporary melting liquid could help build better perovskite solar cells and LEDs
articles.summary: A team co-led by researchers at the University of California San Diego has developed a new way to make perovskite solar cells—a promising next-generation solar technology—more efficient and durable. By creating a temporary liquid while the material crystallizes, researchers were able to grow perovskite crystals that were larger, more uniform and contained fewer defects.
